legal_full:
Preamble. We are building an open map where people around the globe share dosimeter readings for the common good — science, ecology, education, and safety. By publishing your data you help many. Please treat this shared work with care.

1) Responsibility. The accuracy and content of any information you submit remain your responsibility. Data are published and used “as is”. The service does not confirm or guarantee their correctness, completeness, or suitability for any purpose and bears no responsibility for any possible outcome of their use.

2) Openness and license. By sharing dosimetry readings, dates, approximate locations, device models, or other facts, you understand they become available to everyone and may be used freely under the CC0 1.0 (Public Domain) license for data, while the code remains available under the MIT license. Authorship stays with you; no compensation is provided; further redistribution by third parties is beyond our control.

3) “As is” and no verification. Publications appear without prior review. We cannot guarantee instrument calibration or the absence of mistakes. The information is shared for research and is not a professional recommendation.

4) Privacy and moderation. To keep the map safe and trustworthy, timestamps and coordinates may be generalized, and technical metadata may be removed or anonymized. We may hide or delete materials that, in our reasonable opinion, are spam, falsified, unlawful, or disruptive. We handle bona fide measurements with care and strive to preserve them.

5) Cookies. The site relies on a short-lived technical session cookie; it disappears when your visit ends. We do not keep any other traces.

Friends, this map is the result of shared effort and open hearts. Please treat it as a sketch of the terrain, not a precise blueprint. If our work resonates with you, join in — together we can make it better.
legend_full_en:
📍 How to read a radiation map

What matters from the start

  • The number on the map shows only the radiation that the instrument can detect, not the whole radiation risk.
  • Health effects are often linked not to a brief spike but to quiet, long-term exposure that accumulates over months and years.
  • Even a green area can contain hidden sources such as radon, contaminated water, food or airborne particles.
  • The map is a guide, not a guarantee of safety. Use it together with measurements, common sense and, when needed, laboratory testing.
🟩
0–11

Green zone

Generally normal — but not a reason to ignore other sources

0–11 microroentgens per hour is close to typical natural background.

  • Permanent presence is normally acceptable at these readings.
  • Water and locally produced food are usually acceptable, provided there is no separate contamination source.
  • A green reading does not mean zero radiation; it means the measured external level is near the range to which people are normally exposed.
  • Hidden hazards can still include indoor radon, radionuclides in water, food or tobacco.
🟨
11–30

Yellow zone

Pay attention and find the cause

11–30 microroentgens per hour. An immediate hazard is not usually expected, but an isolated yellow patch in a green area deserves investigation.

  • Possible causes include radon, a local source, or alpha/beta contamination that the instrument does not fully register.
  • Check drinking water and food if exposure is regular.
  • Identify the source of the elevated reading and measure indoor radon.
  • Long-term exposure can matter even when there are no immediate symptoms.
🟥
30–100

Red zone

Do not accept the risk without proper checks

30–100 microroentgens per hour should no longer be treated as ordinary background.

  • Avoid permanent residence until the reason is understood.
  • Do not routinely drink local water or eat local food without appropriate testing.
  • Possible causes include man-made radionuclides, contaminated soil and high radon levels in buildings or water.
  • Use tested water and food and make decisions with a clear understanding of the source and duration of exposure.
⬛
100+

Black zone

Prolonged presence is unsafe

More than 100 microroentgens per hour indicates a serious radiation level.

  • Risk can include external irradiation and radionuclides entering the body.
  • Food and water may contain radioactive contaminants even when they look and smell normal.
  • Short-lived elevated readings can occur during air travel or at high altitude, where the exposure situation is different from living in a contaminated area.

🔍 What a dosimeter shows — and what it can miss

Usually detected

  • gamma radiation
  • sometimes part of beta radiation

Often missed or underestimated

  • alpha radiation, especially dangerous when radioactive material enters the body
  • radon in indoor air and water
  • tritium in water and air
  • radionuclides in food
  • neutrons, uncommon but potentially very hazardous
  • A green number therefore does not mean complete safety.

🧬 How radioactive material enters the body

  • Breathing: radon, radioactive dust and smoke can reach the lungs.
  • Water: tritium and dissolved radionuclides can spread through the body.
  • Food: mushrooms, greens, milk and other products can concentrate particular radionuclides.
  • Smoking: tobacco can accumulate radionuclides that are then inhaled.

A brief external exposure or one-time contact is usually less important than repeated or continuous exposure, although the actual risk always depends on dose and radionuclide.

⏳ Time is a major risk factor

Radiation protection follows the ALARA principle: keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable. Repeated moderate exposure can produce a larger cumulative dose than one short-lived rise. Reduce unnecessary time near a source, increase distance where possible and use suitable shielding or other controls.

👥 Who may be more vulnerable

Age, health, pregnancy and individual circumstances can affect sensitivity to radiation. Older people and people with chronic illnesses may have less physiological reserve; children and pregnant people also require particular caution. The same exposure does not have identical consequences for everyone.

⚛️ Radioactive “disguise” inside the body

Some radionuclides behave chemically like familiar substances: tritium follows water, carbon-14 follows carbon, potassium-40 follows potassium, and strontium or radium can follow calcium. The body may incorporate them into tissues, so internal exposure can occur even when an external dosimeter looks normal.

🗺️ Why the map must not be trusted blindly

Even a completely green map shows only part of the situation. It cannot reveal every radionuclide or every exposure route. Treat the map as a prompt to investigate, not as permission to ignore uncertainty: think, measure, verify and ask questions.
legend_safecast_description: This is the traditional radiation level color scale adopted by safecast.org in 2013 and used consistently on their maps since then. Users of safecast.org find it intuitive. The wide color range allows subtle differences to be distinguished instantly at a glance, and the logarithmic scale helps users easily see relatively small differences in radiation levels near natural background while also displaying levels several orders of magnitude higher.

upload_button_tooltip:
Add your measurement track to the map. We support .kml, .kmz, .gpx, .csv, .rctrk, .json, .log, as well as RadiaCode, AtomFast, and SafeCast dosimeters.
If you have another dosimeter or your own log format, write to us on the Chicha Isotope Map project GitHub — we will add support so your measurements can be uploaded to the map.

qr_modal_save_hint: Select the area on the map where the danger was found and create a QR code for that area. Print it and place it at the contamination site — on a fence, tree, or sign next to the object. People will be able to scan the code and immediately see this exact part of the map, the reason for the danger, and take protective measures.
